newsitem.title: UK: UK firms make torture their business - Amnesty.
newsitem.headline: UK firms make torture their business - Amnesty.

text.p: Amnesty International on Tuesday accused Britain of "making death and torture its business" by having secretive and lax export controls on security equipment.

"There is a growing market in riot control and surveillance equipment which has been misused to commit human rights violations and has caused deaths," the international pressure group said in a report.
It said British firms were in the forefront of marketing riot control equipment, razor wire and electrified side panels on security vehicles that would "repulse" demonstrators.
Amnesty, calling on the government to plug legal loopholes, said existing law failed to control sales of equipment brokered by British dealers if the equipment is manufactured abroad.
The report said all export licences should be publicly disclosed in advance. "Without disclosure, parliament has no means to ensure that human rights are protected," it said.

Amnesty said the British government "has failed to establish an effective and transparent mechanism in order to take human rights fully into consideration before authorising military, police and security transfers."
The British government claimed in 1996 that it had been absolved of wrongdoing and vindicated by a three-year inquiry into whether ministers approved illegal sales of arms to Iraq in the mid-1980s.

Trade Secretary Ian Lang said the inquiry by judge Richard Scott, launched by Prime Minister John Major in 1992 after a trial collapsed of three men accused of arms exports to Baghdad, showed ministers had not deliberately misled parliament.
